<!-- Generated by website/sync-docs.py from docs/install/ha-cluster.md. Edit that file, not this one. -->

Three controllers sharing a virtual IP, with etcd. If one goes away, the VIP
moves and the API keeps answering.

This builds on [Proxmox](/docs/install/proxmox/), which covers fetching and checking the
qcow2. Read that first if you have not deployed a single node yet.

## What you need

- Four free addresses on the same segment: one per controller, plus one for the
  virtual IP. They must share a broadcast domain, because VRRP is how the
  controllers agree on who holds it.
- Three free VMIDs.
- 12 GB of RAM and about 96 GB of disk, at the defaults.

## Run it

```bash
DISK_IMAGE=/var/lib/vz/template/corium-0.1.0-x86_64.qcow2 \
SSH_KEY="$(cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub)" \
CLUSTER_NAME=homelab \
VIP=192.168.0.200 \
GATEWAY=192.168.0.1 \
NODE_IPS="192.168.0.201 192.168.0.202 192.168.0.203" \
VMIDS="142 143 144" \
  ./create-ha-cluster.sh
```

`MEMORY`, `CORES` and `DISK_SIZE` default to 4096, 2 and 32G per controller.

**`SSH_KEY` has to be a key this host holds the private half of.** The script
SSHes from the Proxmox node into the controllers to deliver the join token, so
a key from your laptop puts you in the right place with the wrong identity —
the run fails at `Permission denied (publickey)` with three VMs already built.

**The script destroys any VM already holding one of those VMIDs**, unlike
`create-vm.sh` which refuses. Check `qm list` before you run it.

## What it does

A k0s cluster has no pre-shared secret. The first controller generates the
certificate authority, and only once it exists can a join token be minted — so
the other two cannot be configured with a token in advance.

They do not wait on a script for it. Each is given

```yaml
join:
  tokenFrom:
    file: /etc/corium/join-token
    waitFor: 20m
```

so all three boot at once, the two joiners find no token, and they wait. The
script's only job is to deliver one to `/etc/corium/join-token` after the first
controller is answering.

Every controller gets the same VRRP password, generated at run time rather than
defaulted — a shipped default is one everybody keeps, and VRRP authentication
exists precisely to stop a stray host from claiming the VIP. Keepalived uses
only the first eight characters, so it is generated at exactly that length and
Corium rejects anything longer rather than letting controllers disagree about a
password they all believe they set.

Each node is addressed statically, so `NAMESERVER` is set for them. Proxmox's
`ipconfig0` carries an address and a gateway and nothing else; without it the
controllers come up with no resolver and Kubernetes hangs pulling images.

## Check it

```console
$ sudo k0s kubectl get nodes -o wide
NAME              STATUS   ROLES           VERSION       INTERNAL-IP
corium-7c17d087   Ready    control-plane   v1.36.4+k0s   192.168.0.201
corium-87025d9c   Ready    control-plane   v1.36.4+k0s   192.168.0.202
corium-5c5d785f   Ready    control-plane   v1.36.4+k0s   192.168.0.203

$ sudo k0s etcd member-list
{"members":{"corium-5c5d785f":"https://192.168.0.203:2380", ...}}
```

Each node registers **its own address**, not the virtual IP. That distinction
is the difference between a cluster that works and one that works until the
first failover.

The API answers on the VIP, which is what a kubeconfig should point at:

```console
$ curl -sk -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://192.168.0.200:6443/readyz
401
```

401 is the right answer: the server is there and declining an unauthenticated
request.

## Watch it fail over

The address alone will not tell you which controller holds the VIP. ARP will:

```bash
ip neigh flush dev vmbr0
ping -c2 192.168.0.200 >/dev/null
ip neigh show 192.168.0.200        # compare the MAC against each node's
```

Stop that controller and ask again. On a real run the VIP moved within five
seconds, the API kept answering, etcd held quorum at two of three, and the
cluster carried on scheduling. Starting the controller again brought it back
`Ready` inside fifteen seconds.

## When you are done

```bash
for id in 142 143 144; do qm stop "$id"; qm destroy "$id" --purge; done
rm -f /var/lib/vz/snippets/corium-14*.yaml
```

`qm destroy` leaves the cloud-init snippets behind, and the Proxmox host keeps
the controllers' old host keys. Rebuilding onto the same addresses then greets
you with `REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED`, which is alarming and
harmless:

```bash
for ip in 192.168.0.201 192.168.0.202 192.168.0.203; do
  ssh-keygen -f /root/.ssh/known_hosts -R "$ip"
done
```
